ABSTRACT  
Carbon aerogel is an excellent conductive porous carbon material, but suffers from poor mechanical properties 
and fatigue resistance, which greatly limits its application as a flexible electronic device. Herein, the cellulose 
nanofibers/reduced graphene oxide carbon aerogel (BCRCA) with a unique layered structure was prepared by 
bidirectional freezing technique and thermal annealing. BCRCA's layered structure gives it ultra-low density 
(3.25 mg/cm
3
), high specific surface area (159.53 m
2
/g) and good compression properties (91.3 % stress 
retention, 100 cycles at 50 % compression). In addition, BCRCA for supercapacitor electrodes has a high specific 
capacity of 104.3 F g
� 1 
at 0.1 A g
� 1 
and a high capacitance retention rate of 93 % at 5000 cycles at 2 A g
� 1
. 
Notably, the BCRCA assembled into a wearable strain sensor exhibits a stable current signal for real-time 
monitoring of finger, wrist, and elbow joint movements. These advantages make BCRCA have broad applica -
tion prospects in the field of electronic energy storage devices and wearable strain sensors.   
1. Introduction 
Due to the rapid growth of unsustainable consumption and the 
increasing consumption of fossil fuels, environmental problems have 
become increasingly prominent, so new technologies closely related to 
new energy conversion and storage have attracted more and more 
attention [ 1 ]. Among them, the new technologies represented by flexible 
supercapacitors and strain sensors have caused extensive research in 
intelligent robots, intelligent textiles, wearable electronic devices, and 
other advanced fields [ 2 – 4 ]. Lightweight, high power and energy den -
sity, long cycle life, high mechanical flexibility, low cost, high sensitivity 
and fast response speed are the basic requirements of these electronic 
devices [ 5 – 8 ]. For example, smart textiles have high sensitivity and fast 
response ability as multifunctional sensors and heaters for personal 
health management, which was expected to enable disease diagnosis, 
early warning and personal hyperthermia [ 9 ]. 
Carbon aerogels (CAs) are an emerging carbon-based material, 
which is favored by many researchers because of its ultra-high specific 
surface area, rich pore structure and good electrical conductivity 
[ 10 – 12 ]. CAs are usually obtained by carbonizing aerogels in an inert 
atmosphere, and their unique porous structure makes them widely used 
in electromagnetic shielding [ 13 ], sensors [ 14 ], and supercapacitors 
[ 15 ]. However, these carbon aerogels usually have a disordered porous 
structure, which is easy to collapse, and it is difficult to obtain excellent 
compression properties and fatigue resistance [ 16 ]. This is not condu -
cive to the stability and durability of carbon aerogel in practical 
applications. 
Cellulose nanofiber (CNF) is a kind of environment-friendly natural 
polymer material with many advantages, such as stable chemical 
properties, high elastic modulus, and biodegradation [ 17 – 19 ]. The 
unique nanostructure of CNF enables it to be freeze-dried into CNF 
aerogel with a three-dimensional network structure [ 20 ]. After 
carbonization of CNF aerogel under inert gas, carbon aerogel materials 
with conductive properties can be obtained directly. However, pure CNF 
carbon aerogels not only undergo severe volume shrinkage and defor -
mation during the carbonization process, but also it is difficult to pro -
vide satisfactory capacitance by directly using it as an electrode material 
for supercapacitors [ 21 , 22 ]. To solve these problems, CNF is usually

combined with other materials (such as carbon materials [ 23 ], 
conductive polymers [ 24 ], metal compounds [ 25 ], etc.) to prepare 
composite carbon aerogels with excellent conductive and mechanical 
properties. Graphene is a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice structure 
carbon material, which stands out among many carbon materials 
because of its high conductivity and large specific surface area [ 26 ]. 
Unfortunately, the interaction of van der Waals forces and π - π bonds 
between graphene sheets tends to cause the sheets to stack and 
agglomerate [ 27 ]. This seriously hinders electrolyte ion diffusion and 
charge transfer, greatly limiting the further application of graphene in 
supercapacitors and sensor functional devices. Therefore, how to 
reasonably design and use the inherent characteristics and advantages of 
CNF and graphene to build high-performance electronic devices with 
special structures is still a huge challenge. 
Directional freezing is a method for synthesizing bionic porous ma -
terials and bionic layered composites [ 28 ]. Temperature gradient is an 
important factor in directional freezing because it can regulate the di -
rection of ice crystal growth [ 29 ]. Specifically, after the uniform 
colloidal suspension is cooled, the ice crystals gradually nucleate in the 
direction of the temperature gradient. At the same time, solute particles 
are pushed between ice crystals to obtain a oriented structure. In recent 
years, anisotropic aerogels prepared by directional freezing technology 
have been applied in various fields. Compared with traditional random 
freezing, directional freezing aerogels have a suitable microstructure 
and excellent properties [ 30 ]. In this paper, we have carefully designed a 
method to control the nucleation and growth of ice crystals under a 
double temperature gradient to achieve a highly ordered layered 
structure of carbon aerogel. Bidirectional carbon aerogel has more 
outstanding mechanical and electrochemical properties than random 
and single direction carbon aerogel. At the same time, this layered 
structure can generate more conductive paths under pressure, thus 
achieving high sensitivity. Therefore, the dual directional carbon aero -
gel can be effectively used for multifunctional applications in super -
capacitor electrodes and strain sensors. 
Herein, we have prepared a multifunctional nanocellulose/reduced 
graphene oxide carbon aerogel (BCRCA) through a simple bidirectional 
freezing, freeze-drying, and high temperature carbonization strategy. 
BCRCA has ultra-low density and good mechanical compression prop -
erties. Excellent performance is attributed to: (i) CNF acts as a physical 
spacer to effectively prevent the agglomeration of graphene sheets; (ii) 
The two-dimensional carbon skeleton of graphene oxide (GO) can 
reduce the excessive shrinkage of CNF during carbonization and give 
carbon aerogel excellent mechanical strength; (iii) The bidirectional 
freezing method is beneficial for obtaining parallel and ordered lamella, 
effectively achieving stress transfer and electrolyte ion transfer. BCRCA 
as electrode material for supercapacitors has excellent electrochemical 
properties. It also has good sensing performance, can easily monitor 
human activity and shows excellent signal stability. Therefore, the 
BCRCA has excellent application prospects in electrochemical energy 
storage materials and wearable electronic devices. 
2. Experimental section 
2.1. Materials 
CNF dispersion was purchased Zhongshan NanoFC bio-materials Co., 
Ltd. with a concentration of 2.5 %, a width of 35 nm, a length of 1 – 3 μ m, 
and a carboxyl content of 1.02 mmol/g. GO was purchased from Suzhou 
Carbon Peak Graphene Technology Co., Ltd. with a flake diameter of 
0.2 – 10 μ m and a thickness of ~1 nm. Deionized water was prepared by 
laboratory ultrapure water equipment. 
2.2. Preparation of bidirectional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel (BCRCA) 
CNF was first dispersed in deionized water and sonicated in an ice 
bath for 20 min using an ultrasonic cell crusher to obtain a concentration 
of 0.8 wt% CNF suspension. Then, the GO suspension (5 mg/ml) was 
added into the CNF suspension according to the mass ratio of CNF:GO =
1:1, stirring, and ultrasonic 30 min to obtain the mixed suspension. 
Transfer the mixture suspension to the cube plastic mold and place it on 
top of the bidirectional freezing device. The bidirectional freezing de -
vice consists of a curved copper plate immersed in liquid nitrogen at one 
end and hot water at the other (95 
◦
C) to create a temperature gradient. 
After complete freezing, the samples was frozen in a lyophilizer ( � 60 
◦
C, 
1 Pa) for 3 days to obtain CNF/GO aerogel (CGA). Finally, the CGA was 
heated in a tubular furnace at 800 
◦
C under argon for 120 min to obtain 
the layered bidirectional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel, named BCRCA. For 
comparison, unidirectional freezing CNF/RGO carbon aerogel was also 
prepared and named UCRCA (Unidirectional freezing was to place the 
mold on a copper plate and apply liquid nitrogen to the bottom, as 
shown in Fig. S1), and the non-directional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel 
prepared by random freezing in the refrigerator was named NCRCA.

The sample morphology was characterized by environmental scan -
ning electron microscopy (ESEM, Quanta 200, FEI, USA), and the 
microstructure of the sample was observed at an accelerated voltage of 
200 V-30 kV after gold spraying treatment. The diffraction pattern of the 
material was analyzed using a combined multifunctional horizontal X- 
ray diffractometer (XRD Ultima IV, Japan) with an X-ray generator 
power of 3KW, a 2 θ scan range of 10 to 50
◦

◦

2 g, cooling rate < 20 min. The specific surface area and pore size dis -

USA). Degassing temperature: 300 
◦

were compressed and cycled using a mechanical tester equipped with a

2.4. Electrochemical performance measurements 
Electrochemical testing of three types of carbon aerogels BCRCA, 
UCRCA and NCRCA was performed using the electrochemical worksta -
tion of Tatsuwa CHI660E (Shanghai, China). The test system was a 
three-electrode system, and the electrolyte was selected from 1 M 
Na
2
SO
4
. Working electrode: carbon aerogel with a thickness of 2 mm; 
reference electrode: saturated calmel electrode; counter electrode: 
platinum electrode. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge/ 
discharge (GCD) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) 
tests were performed on the two electrodes to compare their electro -
chemical performance excellence. The entire test was conducted at room 
temperature. 
2.5. Sensing performance measurements 
The BCRCA was placed between two copper foils with PE tape, 
assembled into a strain sensor, and connected to the human body's 
finger, wrist and elbow joint. The current change was recorded at the 
electrochemical workstation (CHI660E).

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Preparation and characterization of materials 
The BCRCA synthesis process was shown in Fig. 1 . After evenly 
mixing CNF and GO suspension, BCRCA was prepared by bidirectional 
freezing, freeze-drying, and carbonization. The dual action of hydrogen 
bonding and electrostatic repulsion between CNF and GO results in their 
uniform dispersion in solution. Due to the temperature gradient gener -
ated by bidirectional freezing, the uniformly dispersed CNF and GO 
suspensions were repulsed by the growth of layered ice crystals. Sub -
sequently, these ice crystals were sublimated by freeze-drying to form 
CGA with a regular layered structure. As shown in Fig. 2 a, the pure CNF 
aerogel without GO has a serious volume shrinkage after carbonization, 
while the size shrinkage of CGA with GO was very low after carbon -
ization, which was almost negligible. It was proved that GO can be used 
as a carbon skeleton to prevent the severe volume shrinkage of CNF after 
high temperature carbonization. At the same time, CNF acts as a 
dispersant to prevent agglomeration between graphene sheets. After 
carbonization, the CGA was converted to black BCRCA and retains its 
original shape very well. It can be easily placed on the green leaf without 
making the leaf fall down, indicating that the BCRCA was very light with 
a density of only 3.25 mg/cm
3 
( Fig. 2 b). ESEM observed the detailed 
microstructure of the samples. Under the normal freezing condition of 
the refrigerator, ice crystals grow in both vertical and cross directions, so 
NCRCA exhibits a disordered porous structure inside ( Fig. 2 c). Unidi -
rectional freezing will promote the growth of ice crystals along the 
freezing direction from bottom to vertical. As shown in Fig. 2 d, UCRCA 
has a honeycomb structure with a pore size roughly in the range of 50- 
100 μ m. As expected, the bidirectional frozen BCRCA showed a layered 
structure, with the spacing between adjacent layers at 200 μ m ( Fig. 2 e, 
f), indicating that the problem of graphene sheet aggregation was well 
solved. 
Fig. 3 a showed XRD patterns of CNF, GO, CGA, and BCRCA. The 
diffraction peaks of CNF are 16.2
◦
and 22.3
◦

typical (101) and (200) diffraction planes corresponding to the crystal

◦

CGA showed not only the characteristic peak of CNF but also the char -
acteristic peak of GO, which proved the successful preparation of CGA. 
After high temperature carbonization, the characteristic peak of GO at 
9.6

◦

The specific surface area and pore structure of three carbon aerogels 
with different structures were further evaluated using a specific surface 
area and pore size distribution instrument. Fig. 3 h showed typical ni -
trogen adsorption-desorption isotherms. All carbon aerogels showed 
obvious type IV isotherms, indicating micropores and mesopores [ 40 ]. 
Their specific surface areas and dimensions are shown in Table S1. The 
specific surface area of BCRCA was 159.53 m
2
/g, which was larger than 
the other two carbon aerogels, indicating that more pore structures can 
be formed by the bidirectional freezing method. From the pore size 
distribution curves in Fig. 3 i, we can see that BCRCA's pore size distri -
bution was concentrated in the 2 – 20 nm range, showing a mesoporous 
structure. This pore structure provides rapid ion transport and diffusion, 
effectively reducing resistance and accelerating charge transport [ 41 ]. 
Compression tests investigated the compression properties of the 
carbon aerogel. Fig. 4 a showed the stress-strain curves of BCRCA, 
UCRCA and NCRCA at a strain of 70 %. The stresses of BCRCA, UCRCA 
and NCRCA were 22.7 kPa, 11.7 kPa and 1.5 kPa at 70 % strain. The 
compression properties of BCRCA were much higher than those of the 
other two, because the continuous layered structure formed by bidi -
rectional freeze casting gives carbon aerogel high compression proper -
ties. BCRCA exhibits good compressibility and elasticity at 10 % ~ 70 % 
strain ( Fig. 4 b). The stress-strain curve of BCRCA shows two 
characteristic stages: the first stage was the linear elastic region with ε <
50 %, in which the distance between the sheets decreases and the stress 
increases slowly due to the gradual compression of BCRCA. In the sec -
ond stage, in the densification region of ε > 50 %, the dense accumu -
lation inside BCRCA leads to a significant increase in stress [ 42 ]. Fig. 4 c 
showed cyclic curves for 100 load-unload cycles of BCRCA at 50 % 
strain. After 100 cycles, BCRCA had no obvious plastic deformation and 
stress reduction phenomenon, and the stress retention rate was 91.3 %, 
which indicated that BCRCA had good self-recovery performance and 
stability. Compared to aerogels reported in other literature [ 43 – 51 ], the 
layered BCRCA prepared in this paper exhibit excellent mechanical 
properties ( Fig. 4 d), and have potential application prospects in flexible 
supercapacitors and wearable strain sensors. 
3.2. Electrochemical performance of materials 
Tests were performed in a three-electrode system using BCRCA, 
UCRCA and NCRCA as independent electrodes without the addition of 
any binder or conductive agent. Fig. 5 a – c showed BCRCA, UCRCA and 
NCRCA CV curves at 0 – 1 V voltage window and scan rates of 5, 10, 20, 
50 and 100 mV s
� 1 
scan rates, respectively. At different scanning rates, 
the negative potential scanning direction of BCRCA, UCRCA and NCRCA 
electrodes moves in the positive direction, and the positive potential 
scanning direction moves in the negative direction. The peak current 
was positively correlated with the scanning rate. At the same time, the 
curves were almost symmetrical and approximately rectangular, which 
proves that all three electrodes have good sweep rate capability and 
electric double-layer capacitance performance [ 52 ]. Interestingly, the 
microstructure will affect the capacitive performance of the electrode.

EIS further compared the electrochemical properties of the samples. 
In Fig. 5 h, the Nyquist plots of the BCRCA, UCRCA and NCRCA elec -
trodes all consisted of semicircles in the high-frequency range and 
approximate vertical lines in the low-frequency range. This confirms the 
rapid diffusion of electrolyte ions and low charge transfer resistance, 
showing ideal capacitive performance [ 54 ]. The equivalent series 
resistance (ESR) was expressed as the intercept between the real part of 
the high frequency region and the Nyquist plot. The BCRCA electrode 
ESR of 1.61 Ω was lower than the ESR of 2.95 Ω for the UCRCA electrode 
and 3.26 Ω for the NCRCA electrode. This indicates that the lower in -
ternal resistance of the bidirectional freezing BCRCA electrode can be 
attributed to the layered network structure that promotes the charge 
transfer rate of electrolyte ions. 
Long-term cycle stability was particularly critical to the service life of 
supercapacitor electrode materials. Therefore, we tested the BCRCA 
electrode with 5000 GCD cycles at 2 A g
� 1
( Fig. 5 i). The BCRCA electrode 
has 93 % capacitance retention after 5000 cycles. The better cycling 
stability of BCRCA electrodes was attributed to their large specific sur -
face area and layered properties. The excellent electrochemical prop -
erties and high stability indicate that BCRCA was a potential 
supercapacitor electrode material. 
3.3. Strain sensing performance of BCRCA 
BCRCA's structural advantages and superior compression properties 
make it a promising material for strain sensors. A closed circuit was 
formed at a 9 V power supply, and the LED gradually became brighter as 
the BCRCA was compressed, and the diode became darker when pres -
sure was released ( Fig. 6 a). The reason was due to the gradual reduction 
of the distance between the BCRCA layers during compression, resulting

response characteristics, conductive copper foil tape was placed on both 
ends of the BCRCA in a mechanical test machine and connected to the 
electrochemical workstation with two copper wires (Fig. S4). In the 
range of 10 % ~ 70 % compressive strain, the current increases signif -
icantly with the strain increase and decreases rapidly during the release 
process, indicating that BCRCA had a fast compressive strain current 
response ( Fig. 6 b). As shown in Fig. 6 c, the strain rate was independent 
of the current BCRCA response because the current response remains at 
the same height at different rates, which was crucial for the sensor's 
stability in practical applications. 
Sensitivity was the key factor in evaluating sensor performance. 
BCRCA sensitivity was calculated using the following formula:

0

deformation of BCRCA, the current variation range was small, but suf -

kPa

stage was that many mesoporous pores in BCRCA undergo large 
deformation. This deformation occurs only at higher pressures, resulting 
in high sensitivity. Compared to some other strain sensor sensitivity 
( Fig. 6 e), BCRCA's performance was more outstanding, making it a good 
candidate for strain sensors [ 55 – 60 ]. 
To demonstrate BCRCA's outstanding signal output stability and fa -
tigue, it was cyclically tested at 30 % compression strain. The results in 
Fig. 6 f showed that after 3500 cycles, the sensor signal attenuates very 
little, and the current signal remains almost the same current amplitude 
for each compression cycle. This demonstrates the long operating life 
and high stability of BCRCA for strain sensors, probably due to the high 
stability of the sheet structure. 
BCRCA strain sensor has superior sensing performance and can be 
assembled into a wearable sensor for monitoring the physiological ac -
tivities of the human body. Fig. 7 a showed a schematic diagram of a 
simple sensor device based on BCRCA assembly for human signal 
detection. As shown in Fig. S5, the sensing mechanism was based on the 
change in resistance of the BCRCA during compression. When pressure 
was applied to the BCRCA, the distance between adjacent sheet layers 
gradually decreases and the contact area continuously increases, 
resulting in a tighter conductive network [ 61 ]. The corresponding cur -
rent will increase and the resistance will decrease. When the pressure 
was released, the layer returns to the original structure, and the 
conductive network loosens and the resistance increases. As shown in

BCRCA strain sensor has great application prospects in human activity 
monitoring. 
4. Conclusion 
In summary, we have carefully designed and fabricated a layered 
ultra-light BCRCA with excellent mechanical properties using simple 
and effective bidirectional freeze drying and thermal annealing strate -
gies. BCRCA's rich layered structure facilitates stress transfer and 
diffusion of electrolyte ions. The use of BCRCA for supercapacitor 
electrode materials has good electrochemical properties (104.3 F g 
� 1 
at

� 1

5000 cycles at 2 A g
� 1
). In addition, BCRCA can be used for strain 
sensors with excellent signal stability (3500 cycles) and to monitor 
human activity. In conclusion, this work provides a new way to prepare 
low-cost, sustainable lightweight elastic carbon aerogel, and makes it 
possible to apply it to electronic energy storage devices and wearable 
strain sensors.
